candidate_workflows: When startup costs fall, reassess inherited financing assumptions: start from the capital the company needs and the equity founders are willing to sell instead of an investor's target ownership percentage.
Reduce fundraising transaction cost by precommitting to a check size, standard terms, and a short decision deadline; founders should prioritize investors whose process preserves operating time.
Treat founders as the customers of an investment product: collect recurring complaints, identify the unsatisfied demand behind them, and change the investment process to solve it.
When evaluating investor control, distinguish selection and support from micromanagement; judge the arrangement by whether founder control and aligned service improve company outcomes.
title: Startup Investing Trends

candidate_workflows: Recruit the first users manually, install or onboard them immediately, and track weekly growth; replace manual acquisition only after the startup has momentum and a repeatable path.
Find a promising initial segment by observing which early users are most enthusiastic, then seek more users like them or contain the launch to a narrow market where critical mass is attainable.

For software and other low-error-cost products, launch once the product has a quantum of utility, compensate for incompleteness with unusually attentive service, watch users directly, and turn their friction into product changes; when mistakes carry large penalties, require risk-appropriate validation before exposing users to an incomplete or buggy product.
For hardware or operationally complex products, build or perform the service manually first, record the bottlenecks and tacit lessons, and automate only the workflow the founders now understand.
For B2B discovery, act like an unpaid consultant to one urgent user while keeping a product-company boundary; use the work to find needs shared by adjacent customers.
Treat big launches and large partnerships as suspect when they substitute for founder effort; define every startup idea as both what to build and the unscalable action that gets it moving.
title: Do Things that Don't Scale

candidate_workflows: Before fundraising, test whether the company is a sufficiently good investment bet: require credible founders, a promising market, and stage-appropriate evidence rather than trying to manufacture confidence in a pitch.

Become able to answer detailed market questions, and when an answer is unknown, explain the method for finding it instead of bluffing; raise only after the founders can convince themselves from evidence.
Build the market case as a sequence from a capturable initial segment to a large market, name the external change that makes the opportunity timely, and calibrate proof to the company's age.
After rejection, ask for the actual concern and address it candidly in later conversations, especially when the idea is frightening because it violates conventional assumptions.
Explain the investment case in concise, matter-of-fact language that another partner can accurately retell: make something worth investing in, understand why, and state that truth clearly.
title: How to Convince Investors

candidate_workflows: Expect the first outside commitment to be disproportionately difficult because investors use one another as evidence; keep parallel conversations moving and do not interpret the initial coldness as a verdict on the company.
Treat fundraising popularity as weak evidence of company quality: use commitments to reduce financing risk, not as a success metric or a reason to manufacture a stampede.
If another investor process creates a real deadline, state the timing truthfully without exaggeration and protect each firm's identity unless disclosure is explicitly appropriate.
Raise the price for later money only after risk has genuinely fallen and only with an investor the company can afford to lose; anticipate that some investors will reject changed terms.
title: Investor Herd Dynamics

candidate_workflows: Across fundraising stages, raise only when outside capital will accelerate the company and investors can be convinced; otherwise keep building, because an unsuccessful process consumes time and reputation.

Across stages, protect founder attention by running fundraising as a bounded operating mode: let one founder own and contain it, finish the sprint quickly, and outside that mode accept only money requiring no persuasion or negotiation.

For the phase-2 process analyzed in this essay, build a warm-introduction pipeline, treat every response as no until an unconditional commitment is confirmed, pursue investors in parallel weighted by expected value, and leave every meeting with a concrete next step and timetable.

In phase 2, prioritize a first credible commitment, close committed money into the bank promptly, deprioritize investors who act only after someone else, and prepare capital plans ranging from zero-dollar survival to larger, expense-linked cases.

For phase-2 pricing, optimize first for enough money and second for investor quality rather than headline valuation; establish mutual interest before price and defer high-friction negotiators until terms are anchored.

In phases 2 and later, accept a currently acceptable offer rather than betting on an uncertain better one; phase 1 is different when programs do not decide in parallel, so sequence applications for preferred programs to decide first.

Protect future financing during phase 2 by limiting dilution and keeping the company building, but treat the essay's percentage thresholds, convertible-note mechanics, and anticipated Series A as historically situated rather than universal; recalculate against current instruments and the likely next round.

Assume phase-2 capital may be the last: preserve runway, avoid premature hiring, and enter phase 3 only with evidence that the early experiment worked, usually validated growth or a path to profitability rather than early-stage promise alone.
title: How to Raise Money

candidate_workflows: Pause before trusting ordinary business intuition, but take persistent personal misgivings about a prospective cofounder, employee, investor, or acquirer seriously; work with people known long enough to trust and genuinely like.
Reject startup theater such as fundraising optics, offices, and premature hiring; become expert in users and their problem, and measure progress by whether the product earns love and growth.

Treat founding as an all-consuming, hard-to-reverse commitment; before starting, compare it with the value of broad exploration, and let an unusually strong side project create the reason to narrow focus.

Prepare for ideas and cofounders indirectly: learn consequential domains, work on demanding problems that genuinely interest you with people you respect, and get close enough to a technological or social frontier that missing things become obvious.

Introduce the company-shaped objective late: first follow curiosity and build domain expertise, then recognize which useful side project has become a startup rather than generating plausible-sounding startup ideas on demand.
title: Before the Startup

candidate_workflows: When conflict consumes founder attention, ask whether winning the particular fight advances the general product problem; default to racing ahead through better ideas and execution instead of attacking a rival.
Treat meanness as a startup talent risk: evaluate founder and manager behavior against whether high-optionality people would choose to work with them and stay.
Clarify the nonfinancial purpose that keeps founders building through acquisition opportunities and hard periods; do not assume money alone will sustain the mission.
title: Mean People Fail

candidate_workflows: Flag the fatal-pinch state when runway is short, burn is high, and revenue or agreed progress is weak; assume the probability of rescue financing is zero until money is actually available.

Choose explicitly among shutdown, reaching profitability by cutting burn, or an emergency revenue plan; eliminate nonessential costs and people already known to be wrong before sacrificing strong contributors.

If the company is overhired, shrink to a team that can rediscover the product; if it is already lean, put everyone on the fastest path to revenue and write code only when it directly closes near-term business.

For emergency revenue, ask customers what urgent result they will pay well for, sell a tightly defined derivative of the product, retain the IP, avoid hourly billing, and watch for repeated needs that reveal a scalable product opening.
After any raise, operate as though it is the last: make the company less dependent on investors early enough that survival actions remain reversible.
title: The Fatal Pinch

exclusion_reason: A general reflection on memory, reading, and rereading that does not connect its learning model to a specific startup, maker, team, user, product, work, or communication decision.
title: How You Know

candidate_workflows: Identify which beliefs concern a changing domain, keep them as named working hypotheses, and actively look for environmental changes that would make formerly bad ideas viable.
Avoid rigid forecasts; monitor anomalies, weird hunches, and apparently irrelevant questions from people with deep contact with the domain, then investigate before discounting them.
Turn commentary into recorded bets with decisions and later outcomes so errors create corrective pressure instead of disappearing into conversation.

When the idea is still hard to judge, evaluate whether the people pursuing it are earnest, energetic, and independent-minded, and maintain relationships with people likely to make current expertise obsolete.
title: How to Be an Expert in a Changing World

candidate_workflows: When planning technical hiring, distinguish competent capacity from rare people who can invent otherwise-unimagined solutions; do not assume that more fungible headcount or additional average training substitutes for exceptional capability.

Search globally across programmers, designers, and engineers, and treat immigration friction and talent-hub clustering as first-order recruiting and location constraints when deciding recruiting reach and company location.
title: Let the Other 95% of Great Programmers In

candidate_workflows: Before any corporate-development meeting, answer whether the founders want to sell now and whether an acceptable offer is plausible; if not, decline and state that the team is focused on growth.
Price exploratory acquisition contact by its full attention and morale cost rather than the meeting duration; do not treat flattering interest as a free option.
If the company is neither near death nor strong enough to walk away confidently, protect it from a process designed to create seller momentum, lowball, and renegotiate.
When the decision is genuinely to sell, enter a deliberate M&A process with appropriate techniques; never let the company slide into one through a supposedly casual first meeting.
title: Don't Talk to Corp Dev

candidate_workflows: Inventory difficult tasks that feel rewarding rather than draining, especially ones peers avoid, and use repeated examples as evidence of work for which motivation will compound.
Weight unusually strong or socially odd preferences as higher-signal clues to maker fit, then test them through small real projects instead of relying on job-title introspection.
title: What Doesn't Seem Like Work?

candidate_workflows: Build referral-driven deal flow by treating founders consistently well, following through, and letting a long record of conduct make other participants willing to send their best opportunities.
Evaluate an investor through reports from founders across many deals, especially how the investor behaves when incentives conflict, rather than through friendliness in the current pitch.

Set firm boundaries without opportunistic cruelty: distinguish being good from being a pushover, and behave as though every interaction can become visible and every junior participant may later hold influence.
title: The Ronco Principle

candidate_workflows: When a startup idea sounds small or ridiculous, compare it with the unimpressive starting wedges of successful companies before dismissing it.
Ask what much larger company or platform the current wedge could become, and enumerate the technological, market, or product transitions that make each path plausible.

If several expansion paths survive, pursue the one most immediately compelling to the domain-expert founders while continuing to update the map; do not require an early company to predict its final form.
title: What Microsoft Is this the Altair Basic of?

candidate_workflows: For a US startup without the exact .com matching its company name, treat the mismatch as a possible brand-strength signal and explicitly decide whether the name is worth that cost.
Neutralize identity attachment by imagining the company already had a different name and evaluating whether switching to the current one would still look attractive.
Admit when naming is not a founder strength, enlist someone who has it or generate a large candidate list, and verify domains by actual availability or a quoted asking price before choosing.
Prefer a sufficiently good, controllable name over a supposedly perfect name whose essential asset cannot be acquired; fix the problem while the switching cost remains low.
title: Change Your Name

candidate_workflows: Separate constant-multiple monetization gains from changes in compounding growth rate; model the scenarios before sacrificing user trust for short-term extraction.
Preserve generous behavior when it improves product quality and word-of-mouth, and compensate through disciplined work on growth rather than imitating aggressive business stereotypes.
Treat growth and spending as primary survival variables, while checking the exception where insufficient revenue per customer prevents profitability before runway expires.
title: Why It's Safe for Founders to Be Nice

candidate_workflows: Once the startup has enough operating history, project current revenue growth and constant expenses against cash on hand, and label the company default alive or default dead on a regular cadence.

If default dead, separate facts from hopes in writing: name fundraising as a contingent plan A, specify the exact cost or revenue actions in plan B, and set the date for switching before time runs out.
Do not use hiring to avoid confronting a moderately appealing product; keep the team small enough for founders to evolve the product and use direct, unscalable growth work.
Treat headcount as an effect of validated growth rather than its presumed cause, and resist portfolio-driven advice to scale a business whose economics or appeal are not yet working.
title: Default Alive or Default Dead?
